issue: Source: "with fewer of the benevolent emotions than the latter, are under fewer restraints also". Candidate "and so are under fewer restraints" adds a causal link ("so") the source does not state.
replacement: In the first place, it forfeits the respect and confidence of other nations, and all the advantages that go with a national character. An individual who is seen to be inconstant in his plans, or perhaps to conduct his affairs with no plan at all, is marked at once by all prudent people as a speedy victim of his own unsteadiness and folly. His more friendly neighbors may pity him, but all will decline to link their fortunes with his, and not a few will seize the chance to make their own fortunes out of his. One nation is to another what one individual is to another, with this melancholy difference perhaps: nations have fewer benevolent feelings than individuals, and are also under fewer restraints from taking undue advantage of each other's indiscretions. Every nation, therefore, whose affairs betray a lack of wisdom and stability may expect to suffer every loss that the more systematic policy of its wiser neighbors can inflict. But the best lesson on this subject is, unhappily, given to America by the example of her own situation. She finds that she is held in no respect by her friends, that she is the derision of her enemies, and that she is a prey to every nation that has an interest in speculating on her fluctuating councils and embarrassed affairs.

issue: Source "that diminution of attachment and reverence ... disappoints so many of their flattering hopes". Candidate "the loss of attachment and reverence" overstates a diminution as total loss, and drops "flattering".
replacement: But the most deplorable effect of all is the decline of attachment and reverence that steals into the hearts of the people toward a political system that shows so many marks of weakness and disappoints so many of their flattering hopes. No government, any more than an individual, will long be respected without being truly respectable, and it cannot be truly respectable without a certain measure of order and stability.

issue: Source "answer for places or improvements which could not be accomplished in less than half a dozen years". Candidate "answer for improvements that could not be completed" drops "places".
replacement: To be reasonable, responsibility must be limited to matters within the power of the party held responsible. To be effective, it must relate to operations of that power on which the constituents can readily form a proper judgment. The objects of government may be divided into two general classes. One depends on measures that each have an immediate and noticeable effect. The other depends on a succession of well-chosen and well-connected measures, whose effect is gradual and perhaps unobserved. The importance of the second kind to the collective and lasting welfare of every country needs no explanation. And yet it is clear that an assembly elected for so short a term that it can provide only one or two links in a chain of measures on which the general welfare may essentially depend ought not to answer for the final result. A steward or tenant engaged for one year could not justly be made to answer for estates or improvements that could not be completed in less than half a dozen years. Nor can the people estimate the SHARE of influence that their annual assemblies may each have had on events resulting from the mixed transactions of several years. It is difficult enough to keep the members of a NUMEROUS body personally responsible even for those acts of the body that have an immediate, separate and obvious effect on its constituents.

issue: Source "elected by the people, and REPRESENTING the people in their EXECUTIVE capacity". Candidate turns it into a clumsy relative clause ("officers whom the people elected, who REPRESENTED...") and changes the emphasized word form REPRESENTING to REPRESENTED. Restores the source form.
replacement: Even in the purest democracies of Greece, the people did not carry out many of the executive functions themselves. Those functions were performed by officers elected by the people and REPRESENTING the people in their EXECUTIVE capacity.

issue: Emphasis caps moved. Source "annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE AT LARGE" and "annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE": "annually" is lowercase. Candidate "ELECTED ANNUALLY BY ..." capitalizes ANNUALLY, adding emphasis the source does not have.
replacement: Before the reform of Solon, Athens was governed by nine Archons, annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE AT LARGE. How much power was delegated to them seems to be left in great obscurity. After that period we find an assembly, first of four, and afterward of six hundred members, annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE. It PARTIALLY represented them in their LEGISLATIVE capacity, since its members were not only associated with the people in the function of making laws but also had the exclusive right of originating legislative proposals to the people. The senate of Carthage, too, whatever its power or the length of its appointment, appears to have been ELECTIVE, by the votes of the people. Similar instances might be found in most, if not all, of the popular governments of antiquity.

issue: Emphasis caps moved. Source "annually ELECTED BY THE WHOLE BODY OF THE PEOPLE" and "annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE": ANNUALLY is lowercase in the source; candidate capitalizes it.
replacement: Lastly, in Sparta we meet the Ephori, and in Rome the Tribunes: two bodies, small in numbers, but annually ELECTED BY THE WHOLE BODY OF THE PEOPLE and regarded as the REPRESENTATIVES of the people, almost in a PLENIPOTENTIARY capacity. The Cosmi of Crete were also annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE. Some authors have considered them an institution analogous to those of Sparta and Rome, with this difference only: in electing that representative body, the right to vote was given to only a part of the people.

issue: Hypothesis turned into assertion. Source: "If the observation be well founded, that wise kings will always be served by able ministers, it is fair to argue, that as an assembly of select electors possess...". Candidate: "It is well founded to say that wise kings will always be served by able ministers. It is fair to argue, then, that..." Hamilton-style qualification (Jay here) removed; the premise is stated as fact.
replacement: The select assemblies that choose the President, like the State legislatures that appoint the senators, will in general be composed of the most enlightened and respectable citizens. There is reason to presume, therefore, that they will direct their attention and their votes only to those men who have become most distinguished for their abilities and virtue, and in whom the people see just grounds for confidence. The Constitution shows very particular attention to this object. It excludes men under thirty-five from the first office and those under thirty from the second. In this way it confines the electors to men of whom the people have had time to form a judgment, and with respect to whom they will not be liable to be deceived by those brilliant displays of talent and patriotism which, like passing meteors, sometimes mislead as well as dazzle. If it is well founded to say that wise kings will always be served by able ministers, it is fair to argue that an assembly of select electors has, in a greater degree than kings, the means of broad and accurate information about men and characters, and so their appointments will show at least equal discretion and discernment. The natural inference from these considerations is that the President and senators so chosen will always be among those who best understand our national interests, whether in relation to the individual States or to foreign nations; who are best able to promote those interests; and whose reputation for integrity inspires and deserves confidence. With such men the power of making treaties may safely be lodged.

issue: Emphasis capitals lost. Source "his more CONCEITED NEIGHBOR"; candidate "his more CONCEITED neighbor". NEIGHBOR must stay capitalized.
replacement: But suppose one or the other of the substitutes we have examined, or some other that might be devised, were thought preferable in this respect to the plan reported by the Convention. It would not follow that the Constitution ought for that reason to be rejected. If mankind were to resolve to agree on no institution of government until every part of it had been adjusted to the most exact standard of perfection, society would soon become a general scene of anarchy and the world a desert. Where is the standard of perfection to be found? Who will undertake to bring the clashing opinions of a whole community to the same judgment of it, and to persuade one conceited projector to give up his INFALLIBLE criterion for the FALLIBLE criterion of his more CONCEITED NEIGHBOR? To serve the purpose of the adversaries of the Constitution, they ought to prove, not merely that particular provisions in it are not the best that could have been imagined, but that the plan on the whole is bad and destructive.

issue: "least inconvenience" keeps the archaic sense; STYLE-NOTE renders inconvenience as problem/drawback.
replacement: A SECOND objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is that it contributes to an undue accumulation of power in that body, tending to give the government too aristocratic an appearance. The Senate, it is observed, is to have concurrent authority with the Executive in making treaties and in appointing to offices. If, say the objectors, the power of deciding all cases of impeachment is added to these prerogatives, it will give senatorial influence a decided predominance. To an objection so imprecise in itself, it is not easy to give a very precise answer. Where is the measure or standard to which we can appeal in deciding what will give the Senate too much influence, too little, or barely the proper amount? Would it not be both safer and simpler to dismiss such vague and uncertain calculations, to examine each power by itself, and to decide on general principles where it may be placed with the most advantage and the least drawback?

issue: STYLE-NOTE fixed term: "chief magistrate" -> "chief executive" (the President). Source "the Chief Magistrate of the Union" is the President; candidate leaves "Chief Magistrate", which a modern reader hears as a judge.
replacement: The security the Constitution essentially intends against corruption and treachery in making treaties is to be sought in the numbers and characters of those who are to make them. The JOINT AGENCY of the Chief Executive of the Union and of two thirds of the members of a body selected by the collective wisdom of the legislatures of the individual States is designed to be the pledge for the fidelity of the national councils in this matter. The Convention might properly have intended the punishment of the Executive for departing from the instructions of the Senate, or for lack of integrity in conducting the negotiations entrusted to him. It might also have had in view the punishment of a few leading individuals in the Senate who had prostituted their influence in that body as the mercenary instruments of foreign corruption. But it could not, with more or even equal propriety, have contemplated the impeachment and punishment of two thirds of the Senate for consenting to an improper treaty, any more than of a majority of that branch or of the other branch of the national legislature for consenting to a harmful or unconstitutional law. That is a principle which, I believe, has never been admitted into any government. How, in fact, could a majority in the House of Representatives impeach themselves? Not better, it is evident, than two thirds of the Senate could try themselves. And yet what reason is there that a majority of the House of Representatives, sacrificing the interests of society by an unjust and tyrannical act of legislation, should escape with impunity any more than two thirds of the Senate, sacrificing the same interests in an injurious treaty with a foreign power? The truth is that in all such cases it is essential to the freedom and the necessary independence of the body's deliberations that its members be exempt from punishment for acts done in a collective capacity. The security of society must depend on the care taken to place the trust in proper hands, to make it their interest to execute it faithfully, and to make it as difficult as possible for them to combine in any interest opposed to the public good.
